architectural_implications.after: Engineer or coding agent pulls production traces via CLI, clusters failures, and derives fix candidates from observed behavior.
architectural_implications.before: Engineer reads code and reproduces the bug locally to guess what happened.
architectural_implications.consequence: The observability platform's CLI/tool API becomes a load-bearing developer interface; its ergonomics and data fidelity determine debugging speed.
architectural_implications.observation: Improvement loop runs on traces pulled out of the observability backend into a coding agent, rather than on the source repo alone.

architectural_implications.after: Eval cases harvested from failing production traces and versioned alongside experiment runs.
architectural_implications.before: Eval sets written up front from imagined user inputs.
architectural_implications.consequence: Eval quality tracks traffic coverage; requires governance for PII handling, sampling, and re-baselining as distributions shift.
architectural_implications.observation: Evaluators and datasets become derived artifacts of production traffic rather than hand-written specs.

architectural_implications.after: Agent must traverse observe -> cluster -> hypothesize -> evaluate -> fix -> experiment -> verify before a change is accepted.
architectural_implications.before: Prompt an agent to 'fix the bug' with no evidence discipline.
architectural_implications.consequence: Reliability comes from the loop scaffold and the verification gate, not from model capability; the harness becomes the thing to engineer and test.
architectural_implications.observation: The coding agent is given a bounded, repeatable procedure (the 8-step loop) plus tools, rather than open-ended license to fix.

article_ideas.angle: Reframe the tooling market and the engineering job description: measure teams by time-from-symptom-to-evaluator, not by dashboard coverage or span volume.
article_ideas.audience: AI platform leads and evaluation engineers deciding where to invest next quarter
article_ideas.based_on: You know your agent is broken long before you know how to evaluate the failure.
article_ideas.thesis: Instrumentation is a solved commodity; the binding constraint on agent quality is the latency between noticing a failure and encoding it as an executable check. Teams that buy dashboards without buying an evaluator-authoring workflow will observe their failures indefinitely without regressing them.
article_ideas.title: You Already Know It's Broken: The Bottleneck Is Evaluator Authoring, Not Observability

article_ideas.angle: Architectural argument with a concrete consequence: any debugging tool that cannot consume spans is unusable on agents, regardless of how good its code analysis is.
article_ideas.based_on: You cannot read an agent or harness through code alone
article_ideas.thesis: When control flow is decided at runtime by a model, the trace — not the repository — is the artifact that specifies actual behavior. Debuggers, tests, and coding agents must therefore take traces as their primary input interface, which makes span-level capture a prerequisite for debugging rather than an observability afterthought.
article_ideas.title: Traces Are the Source Code of an Agent

article_ideas.angle: Failure-taxonomy piece: walk a single refund/order-status misroute through every conventional check it passes, then show what a trajectory-level judge or precondition contract would have caught.
article_ideas.based_on: A customer asked for a refund, but the support agent called `get_order_status`
article_ideas.thesis: As agents compose tools, the dominant reliability risk migrates from crashes and schema violations to plausible-but-wrong action selection that returns a well-formed, confident, incorrect answer. Output-level validation and exception handling are structurally blind to this class, so correctness must be judged at the trajectory level.
article_ideas.title: Silent Tool Routing Is the New Outage — and Your Validators Can't See It

article_ideas.angle: Argue the harness is the artifact to engineer, version, and test; treat prompt-and-pray 'fix the bug' instructions as the anti-pattern.
article_ideas.audience: Teams building internal agentic developer tooling
article_ideas.based_on: The agent doesn't magically fix everything. It just follows the loop a good engineer would.
article_ideas.thesis: The reliability of agent-driven debugging comes from the enforced procedure — observe, cluster, hypothesize, evaluate, fix, experiment, verify — plus a verification gate, not from model capability. This is testable and consequential: swap the model and loop completion rate should hold, while removing the gate should cause regressions to ship faster.
article_ideas.title: Your Agent Debugger Is a Scaffold, Not a Genius

connections.relationship: Production traces are the raw material from which eval cases and judges are derived, making observability upstream of evaluation.
Clusters define the unit of coverage; each cluster ideally maps to one dataset slice and one evaluator.
Exposing backend capabilities as agent-drivable commands is what lets a coding agent act as the debugger.
Treats agent debugging as a repeatable pipeline with a verification gate, analogous to build-test-ship.
Semantic correctness of tool choice and of the resulting answer must be judged at the trajectory level, not the output level.

evidence_quotes.text: You know your agent is broken long before you know how to evaluate the failure.

core_insights.generalization: For any non-deterministic system, the expensive step is operationalizing a quality criterion, not observing anomalies — build the path from observed failure to codified check as a first-class workflow.
core_insights.insight: Failure detection and failure evaluation are decoupled in time: engineers observe that an agent is broken well before they can formalize what 'broken' means as a metric, so the operational bottleneck is converting a felt symptom into an executable evaluator rather than detecting the symptom.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Shifts effort from monitoring/dashboards toward evaluator authoring as the scarce engineering activity; teams that only instrument will still stall because they cannot regression-test the failure they just saw.

evidence_quotes.text: You cannot read an agent or harness through code alone; traces provide the execution context needed to find root causes.
LLM agents have non-linear execution paths requiring deep traces.

core_insights.generalization: When control flow is decided at runtime by a model, the execution record becomes the primary specification of behavior; debuggers, tests, and agents must all consume traces as their input interface.
core_insights.insight: Traces occupy the architectural role that call graphs/APM occupy in deterministic software: because agent execution paths are non-linear and reasoning-mediated, the trace — not the source code — is the artifact that must be read to locate a root cause.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Implies tracing is a prerequisite for debugging, not a nice-to-have: without span-level capture of every tool call and LLM response, no amount of code reading localizes the fault.

evidence_quotes.text: Setting up CLI skills enables the coding agent to act as an automated debugger.

core_insights.generalization: Agentic tooling is most powerful when the observability backend exposes a programmatic CLI/skill surface that an agent can drive, rather than a human-only UI.
core_insights.insight: The debugging loop is externalized as an installable skill that a coding agent executes against production trace data via a CLI, so the agent — not the human — performs trace pulling, failure clustering, hypothesis formation, evaluator authoring, and fix proposal.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Moves the debugging harness outside the application codebase and into a tool-interface layer (CLI + skill), making the improvement loop scriptable, repeatable, and transferable across projects.

evidence_quotes.text: Pulling production traces, clustering failures, forming hypotheses, running evaluators, proposing fixes, and running experiments.

core_insights.generalization: Any evaluation pipeline over high-volume production traffic needs a clustering/dedup stage before human or agent analysis, or cost scales with incident count rather than with distinct causes.
core_insights.insight: Failure clustering is the compression primitive that makes the loop tractable: instead of debugging individual bad outputs, related failures are grouped so that one root-cause hypothesis and one evaluator cover a whole class of production errors.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Converts unbounded per-incident debugging into a bounded number of clusters, which is the mechanism behind the claimed days-to-minutes compression.

core_insights.generalization: Evaluation suites degrade when they drift from observed traffic; the sustainable pattern is continuous harvesting of real traces into eval datasets plus baseline-vs-candidate experiment runs.
core_insights.insight: Evaluators should be authored against real production trajectories rather than synthetic inputs, with experiments comparing a candidate against a stored baseline and runnable either locally or on the platform.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Makes the eval dataset a production-derived artifact that stays distributionally aligned with the failures actually occurring, and makes experiment comparison the acceptance gate for fixes.

evidence_quotes.text: A customer asked for a refund, but the support agent called `get_order_status` instead and incorrectly claimed the refund was already issued.

core_insights.generalization: As agents compose tools, the dominant reliability risk migrates from crashes/schema errors to plausible-but-wrong action selection, requiring trajectory-level judges rather than output-level validation.
core_insights.insight: A representative agent failure is a silent semantic routing error — the agent invokes a plausible but wrong tool (`get_order_status` for a refund request) and then fabricates a successful-looking answer, which no exception, schema check, or output-format validator would catch.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Argues that tool-selection correctness and groundedness must be evaluated as semantic properties of the trajectory, since the failure surfaces as a confident, well-formed response.

evidence_quotes.text: You cannot read an agent or harness through code alone; traces provide the execution context needed to find root causes.
LLM agents have non-linear execution paths requiring deep traces.
Traces capture every step, tool call, and LLM response.

deep_dives.research_question: Which subset of captured span fields (tool name, tool arguments, tool result, model reasoning, intermediate state, latency, token counts) is minimally sufficient for a human or coding agent to correctly localize the root cause of an agent failure?
deep_dives.topic: Minimum viable trace schema for root-cause localization
deep_dives.trigger_insight: What is the minimum trace schema and span granularity needed
deep_dives.why: If a small set of fields carries almost all localization signal, tracing cost, storage, and PII surface can be cut dramatically; if reasoning text is load-bearing, redaction and retention policies must change. Without an ablation, teams instrument maximally and still cannot tell which fields made the debug succeed.

evidence_quotes.text: A customer asked for a refund, but the support agent called `get_order_status` instead and incorrectly claimed the refund was already issued.
What are the best guardrails to prevent silent tool failures?
How do we balance the cost of running LLM-as-a-judge evaluators against accuracy?

deep_dives.research_question: Can wrong-tool-invocation failures be detected structurally — via intent-to-tool contracts and argument preconditions — with recall comparable to an LLM judge at materially lower cost?
deep_dives.topic: Deterministic tool-call preconditions versus LLM-judge tool-selection evaluators
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Can tool-selection correctness be verified structurally rather than by an LLM judge?
deep_dives.why: The most dangerous failure returns HTTP 200 with a confident, well-formed, wrong answer, so exception handling and schema validators are structurally blind to it. If deterministic preconditions catch most of these, judge capacity is freed for genuinely semantic properties like groundedness; if they do not, teams must budget judge calls on every tool call, not every conversation.

evidence_quotes.text: Set up evaluators that run against real production traces.
Evaluations can be run locally or via the platform to compare baselines against candidates.
Fewer failures occur with each iteration pass.

deep_dives.research_question: How quickly does an eval set harvested from a fixed window of failing production traces stop discriminating on fresh traffic, and what re-baselining cadence keeps it predictive?
deep_dives.topic: Memorization risk in eval suites harvested from production failures
deep_dives.trigger_insight: How do you prevent eval suites harvested from production failures from overfitting to past incidents?
deep_dives.why: The loop claims convergence ('fewer failures occur with each iteration pass'), but a harvested eval set is a sample of past incidents. If it saturates, the verification gate passes candidates that would fail on new traffic — the loop appears to converge while production quality plateaus. This determines whether continuous harvesting is optional hygiene or a mandatory control.

evidence_quotes.text: The agent doesn't magically fix everything. It just follows the loop a good engineer would.
Setting up CLI skills enables the coding agent to act as an automated debugger.
Automating the loop compresses days of debugging into minutes.

deep_dives.research_question: What experiment delta and guardrail-eval combination is sufficient to auto-accept an agent-proposed prompt or code change, and at what point must a human reviewer enter the loop?
deep_dives.topic: Acceptance thresholds as automated merge gates for agent-proposed fixes
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Who owns the fix when a coding agent proposes changes
deep_dives.why: The claimed days-to-minutes compression depends entirely on the verify step, which the summary leaves unspecified. If the gate is too loose, the loop ships plausible-but-wrong fixes faster than a human team would; too tight and the compression vanishes. This is the boundary between a demo and a deployable practice.

evidence_quotes.text: Pulling production traces, clustering failures, forming hypotheses, running evaluators, proposing fixes, and running experiments.
Every failure runs the same loop: observe, evaluate, and develop.
Fewer failures occur with each iteration pass.

deep_dives.research_question: In real agent traffic, how concentrated is the failure distribution across root-cause clusters — is the number of distinct causes bounded and stable, or does it grow with incident count and defeat the clustering compression?
deep_dives.topic: Failure-cluster size distribution as the precondition for loop tractability
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Agent failures are systematic enough to be clustered into a small number of root causes.
deep_dives.why: The entire days-to-minutes claim rests on one hypothesis and one evaluator covering a whole class of errors. If the distribution is heavy-tailed with mostly singleton clusters, per-incident cost is irreducible and the loop's throughput advantage disappears — a result worth knowing before teams reorganize around cluster-driven triage.

project_ideas.name: Span Ablation Bench
project_ideas.poc: Freeze a corpus of 60-100 labeled agent failures with known root causes. Programmatically produce five trace projections (minimal, +reasoning, +args, +intermediate state, full). Have both a coding agent and human engineers localize root causes under each projection, blind to the label.

project_ideas.based_on: Can tool-selection correctness be verified structurally rather than by an LLM judge?
project_ideas.hypothesis: Deterministic intent-to-tool preconditions and argument constraints detect at least 60% of silent wrong-tool-invocation failures at under 5% of the cost of an LLM-judge tool-selection evaluator.
project_ideas.measurement: Recall and precision against labeled misroutes, false-positive rate on clean traffic, cost per 1k tool calls, and latency added per call. Falsified if recall trails the judge by more than 20 points or false positives exceed 3%.
project_ideas.name: Tool Contract Linter
project_ideas.poc: Define declarative preconditions per tool (e.g. refund path requires a refund-intent signal and a refund-eligible order state). Run the linter and a judge evaluator over a corpus containing the refund/order-status misroute class plus clean traffic, and compare detection sets.

project_ideas.based_on: How do you prevent eval suites harvested from production failures from overfitting to past incidents?
project_ideas.hypothesis: Eval suites harvested from a single traffic window lose at least 30% of their discriminating power on traffic sampled four weeks later, even with no code changes.
project_ideas.measurement: Discrimination (AUC or pass-rate gap between known-good and known-bad outputs) per window, plus the week at which the gate fails to flag a deliberately injected regression. Falsified if discrimination holds within 10% across four weeks.
project_ideas.name: Eval Decay Monitor
project_ideas.poc: Harvest a failure-derived eval set from week 0 traffic. Replay baseline, week-2, and week-4 traffic windows through the same agent build and score each window with the week-0 evaluators; also track candidate-vs-baseline deltas per window to see when the gate stops separating good from bad.

project_ideas.based_on: Agent failures are systematic enough to be clustered into a small number of root causes.
project_ideas.hypothesis: Real agent failure traffic compresses into a bounded set of root-cause clusters such that the top 20 clusters cover at least 70% of incidents, making cluster-driven triage cheaper than per-incident debugging.
project_ideas.measurement: Cluster-size distribution (share of incidents in top 20), cluster purity from human labels, number of distinct root causes per cluster, and estimated engineer-hours saved versus incident-by-incident triage. Falsified if top-20 coverage falls below 50% or average purity drops under 0.7.
project_ideas.name: Cluster Compression Audit
project_ideas.poc: Ingest a month of production traces for an agent, run embedding-plus-LLM clustering on failure outputs and trajectories, then have engineers label a stratified sample to measure cluster purity and how many distinct causes sit behind the top clusters.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Ankur Duggal
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Evaluating and improving AI agents using traces, CLIs, and structured loops
  • Purpose: To demonstrate a structured, repeatable framework for debugging and evaluating AI agents in production using observability tools and coding agent skills. Ankur Duggal from Arize AI explains how developers can move beyond debugging AI agents on vibes and establish rigorous evaluation loops using traces, datasets, root-cause analysis, and experiment management. He demonstrates setting up a coding agent skill via the Arize CLI to automatically pull traces, cluster failures, and propose code and prompt fixes.

Topic Map

The Problem with Vibing in Agent Development

  • Explanation: Many developers ship AI agents based on gut feelings or basic input-output checks, which fails in production when edge cases arise.
  • Key claims:
    • Most developers ship agents based on vibes.
    • Gut feeling is insufficient for production-grade AI applications.
    • Agents are non-deterministic, making evaluation extremely difficult.
  • Examples:
    • Checking answers manually by prompting the agent and hoping it looks correct.
  • Terminology:
    • vibe debugging
    • evals
    • production failure
  • Why it matters: Without proper evaluations, developers cannot reliably catch errors or trust their AI agents in production.

Traces as the New Source of Truth

  • Explanation: Unlike traditional software with deterministic call graphs, AI agents rely on LLM reasoning steps that require tracing to debug.
  • Key claims:
    • Traditional software has deterministic paths that are easy to trace via APM tools.
    • LLM agents have non-linear execution paths requiring deep traces.
    • Traces capture every step, tool call, and LLM response.
  • Examples:
    • A support agent calling the wrong order status tool due to hallucination.
  • Terminology:
    • traces
    • APM monitoring
    • tool call
    • groundedness
  • Why it matters: You cannot read an agent or harness through code alone; traces provide the execution context needed to find root causes.

The 8-Step Failure Loop

  • Explanation: A systematic engineering loop for moving from a production failure to a verified improvement in minutes rather than days.
  • Key claims:
    • Every failure runs the same loop: observe, evaluate, and develop.
    • Fewer failures occur with each iteration pass.
    • Automating the loop compresses days of debugging into minutes.
  • Examples:
    • Pulling production traces, clustering failures, forming hypotheses, running evaluators, proposing fixes, and running experiments.
  • Terminology:
    • failure cluster
    • root-cause hypothesis
    • evaluator
    • experimentation
  • Why it matters: Structured loops prevent developers from chasing failures manually and speed up the feedback loop.

Live Demo: Connecting to a Coding Agent

  • Explanation: Demonstrating how to install the Arize CLI and connect a coding agent (like Claude Code) to analyze traces, cluster failures, and run experiments.
  • Key claims:
    • Setting up CLI skills enables the coding agent to act as an automated debugger.
    • The agent pulls traces, clusters errors, and suggests prompt or code fixes.
    • Evaluations can be run locally or via the platform to compare baselines against candidates.
  • Examples:
    • Running ax tool install arize-ax-cli to enable coding agent debugging skills.
  • Terminology:
    • AX CLI
    • coding agent
    • evaluators
    • datasets
  • Why it matters: Automating trace analysis and experiment generation drastically cuts down the engineering overhead of fixing agent bugs.

Key Points

Shift from vibe debugging to metric-driven evaluations

  • Explanation: Relying on intuition in production leads to undetected hallucinations and systemic failures.
  • Evidence: Audience poll showed high adoption of vibe-based checking compared to structured evaluation setups.
  • Practical implication: Teams must build eval suites tied to real production traces.

Traces reveal hidden agent execution errors

  • Explanation: Agentic workflows make multiple tool calls and reasoning steps that require step-by-step visibility.
  • Evidence: An example trace showed a support agent calling order status instead of handling a refund request.
  • Practical implication: Instrumentation is mandatory before attempting to debug complex multi-step agents.

Agents follow an engineering loop, not magic

  • Explanation: Fixing agents requires gathering evidence, forming hypotheses, writing evals, testing prompts, and verifying results.
  • Evidence: The 8-step loop framework demonstrated at Arize.
  • Practical implication: Engineering teams should treat agent debugging with the same rigor as CI/CD pipelines.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The 8-Step Failure Loop

  • How it works: A systematic workflow to take a production failure, trace it, cluster issues, test hypotheses, build evaluators, apply code/prompt fixes, run experiments, and verify improvements.
  • Components:
    • Production failure
    • Trace evidence
    • Failure cluster
    • Root-cause hypothesis
    • Evaluator
    • Code / prompt fix
    • Experiment
    • Verified improvement
  • When to use: Whenever an AI agent fails in production and needs systematic debugging and evaluation.

Examples & Case Studies

A customer asked for a refund, but the support agent called get_order_status instead and incorrectly claimed the refund was already issued.

  • Illustrates: Tool selection failure and hallucination in production agents.
  • Lesson: Tracing is necessary to catch incorrect tool routing and faulty reasoning steps.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Install the Arize CLI to connect your coding agent to trace data.
    • Set up evaluators that run against real production traces.
  • Strategic:
    • Shift away from vibe-based shipping toward rigorous evaluation loops.
    • Integrate APM telemetry, codebases, and engineering tickets into your debugging workflow.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How do we balance the cost of running LLM-as-a-judge evaluators against accuracy?
    • What are the best guardrails to prevent silent tool failures?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • 44% of agent interactions resulted in bad summaries in the demo financial agent example. (statistic)
  • Connecting coding agents to CLI skills reduces debugging time from days to minutes. (productivity claim)

Notable Quotes

"You know your agent is broken long before you know how to evaluate the failure." "The agent doesn't magically fix everything. It just follows the loop a good engineer would."

Compressed Summary

  • Avoid shipping AI agents based purely on vibe checks.
  • Use traces as the new source of truth for non-deterministic agent workflows.
  • Implement a structured 8-step failure loop for evaluating and fixing agents.
  • Leverage CLI coding agent skills to automate trace analysis and experiment generation.
  • Keywords: evaluation, tracing, agents, debugging, observability
  • Core insight: AI agents are not magic; debugging them successfully requires moving from gut feelings to structured trace-based evaluation loops.

- **Explanation**: Relying on intuition in production leads to undetected hallucinations and systemic failures.
- **Evidence**: Audience poll showed high adoption of vibe-based checking compared to structured evaluation setups.
- **Practical implication**: Teams must build eval suites tied to real production traces.
### Traces reveal hidden agent execution errors
- **Explanation**: Agentic workflows make multiple tool calls and reasoning steps that require step-by-step visibility.
- **Evidence**: An example trace showed a support agent calling order status instead of handling a refund request.
- **Practical implication**: Instrumentation is mandatory before attempting to debug complex multi-step agents.
### Agents follow an engineering loop, not magic
- **Explanation**: Fixing agents requires gathering evidence, forming hypotheses, writing evals, testing prompts, and verifying results.
- **Evidence**: The 8-step loop framework demonstrated at Arize.
- **Practical implication**: Engineering teams should treat agent debugging with the same rigor as CI/CD pipelines.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### The 8-Step Failure Loop
- **How it works**: A systematic workflow to take a production failure, trace it, cluster issues, test hypotheses, build evaluators, apply code/prompt fixes, run experiments, and verify improvements.
- **Components**:
  - Production failure
  - Trace evidence
  - Failure cluster
  - Root-cause hypothesis
  - Evaluator
  - Code / prompt fix
  - Experiment
  - Verified improvement
- **When to use**: Whenever an AI agent fails in production and needs systematic debugging and evaluation.
## Examples & Case Studies
### A customer asked for a refund, but the support agent called `get_order_status` instead and incorrectly claimed the refund was already issued.
- **Illustrates**: Tool selection failure and hallucination in production agents.
- **Lesson**: Tracing is necessary to catch incorrect tool routing and faulty reasoning steps.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Install the Arize CLI to connect your coding agent to trace data.
  - Set up evaluators that run against real production traces.
- **Strategic**:
  - Shift away from vibe-based shipping toward rigorous evaluation loops.
  - Integrate APM telemetry, codebases, and engineering tickets into your debugging workflow.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How do we balance the cost of running LLM-as-a-judge evaluators against accuracy?
  - What are the best guardrails to prevent silent tool failures?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- 44% of agent interactions resulted in bad summaries in the demo financial agent example. (statistic)
- Connecting coding agents to CLI skills reduces debugging time from days to minutes. (productivity claim)
## Notable Quotes
> "You know your agent is broken long before you know how to evaluate the failure."
> "The agent doesn't magically fix everything. It just follows the loop a good engineer would."
## Compressed Summary
- Avoid shipping AI agents based purely on vibe checks.
- Use traces as the new source of truth for non-deterministic agent workflows.
- Implement a structured 8-step failure loop for evaluating and fixing agents.
- Leverage CLI coding agent skills to automate trace analysis and experiment generation.
- **Keywords**: evaluation, tracing, agents, debugging, observability
- **Core insight**: AI agents are not magic; debugging them successfully requires moving from gut feelings to structured trace-based evaluation loops.
